summary: This article, dated September 25, 2023, argues that folklore about sacred places and enchanted landscapes is a living tradition that persists in the modern world. It surveys examples from Mount Kailash, Stonehenge, Norwegian fjords, the Amazon, Ireland, Sedona and Japan. It also covers the role of technology, conservation, education, digital archives and science in preserving and understanding these places. The article ends without a conclusion.
one_line: A 2023 article on how sacred sites and enchanted landscapes keep folklore alive through technology, conservation, education, digital archiving and science.
key_facts: The article is dated September 25, 2023 and presents folklore as a living, evolving tradition rather than a relic of the past.
Mount Kailash in Tibet is revered by multiple religions as the abode of gods and pivot of the universe.
Archaeologist Liam O'Connell's recent study suggests Stonehenge is aligned with various celestial events.
'Nøkken' is a water spirit of the Norwegian fjords said to lurk in the depths and enchant unwary travelers with his violin.

Marco Silva, a tech entrepreneur, introduced 'Augmented Reality Folklore Trails', which superimpose digital narratives onto physical landscapes via a user's smartphone and attract a younger demographic.
'The Global Folklore Initiative' launched on September 7, 2023, spearheaded by cultural envoy David Kim, and includes a vast digital library of myths from many cultures.

The Kumbh Mela in India is a mass Hindu pilgrimage that draws millions toward the sacred rivers; sociologist Martin Hughes says such gatherings transmit collective memory and values across generations.
UNESCO declared the ancient forest of Daintree in Australia a 'Heritage Conservation Zone' on December 10, 2023.
Conservationist Angela Nguyen leads a community-driven project in Daintree to protect the landscape and digitally archive the dreamtime stories of the Aboriginal people connected to the forest.
Educator Thomas Hill launched the 'Mythic Minds' program on November 5, 2023, to integrate local and global folklore into school curricula.
Digital librarian Emma Larson works with communities worldwide to record and transcribe oral traditions associated with sacred places.
Dr. Robert Chen, a geologist using LIDAR technology, mapped topographic changes that corroborate the ancient flood myths of various cultures.
Dr. Emily Watson of the University of Ancient Lore says sacred sites are 'anchors, connecting the tangible and the spiritual'.
The article lacks a conclusion; the final section is cut off and ends with a note saying no conclusion was included.
